citations.text: I inspected the original scan pixels. The headword is 百; the entry identifies oracle-bone examples as 商, then catalogs Zhou, Spring and Autumn, Warring States, transmitted Shuowen, and Han forms. The author calls 百 a “special phonetic” character: its account reads the Shang form as 白 with an added indicative mark and says 白 also supplies sound. It proposes that 白 was the source, sound, and initial graph for 百, first used for the numeral and later differentiated by a dedicated graph. This is the book’s attributed analysis, not a settled graphic history. The entry also reports one hundred as the basic sense and cites oracle-bone and Western Zhou bronze examples, plus examples it interprets as large quantity. I checked the entry through its end on this page; the following page is not a continuation of the 百 entry.

citations.field: 百 headword; PDF p. 303, printed p. 291; same scan provenance as preceding record
citations.text: The scan’s formation discussion distinguishes its proposed sound role from the lower form’s graphic identity. It says the upper mark is an indicative sign, but describes the lower form in its historical account as 白 (zì, a corruption of 白) and elsewhere says 白’s component in later forms is corrupted as 自. The surrounding prose attributes these readings to the book; the atypical historical shapes should remain occurrence-bound rather than be silently normalized to a Unicode character. This account is distinct from analyses that treat the upper stroke as 一 in a combined 一百 spelling.
